KEY MESSAGE 1...

A quasi-stationary frontal boundary continues to meander north
of the region this morning across the northern Ohio Valley,
resulting in another mainly clear and quiet morning across the
forecast area, albeit 5-10 degrees warmer than that of
yesterday. A WSW to W low-level feed continues to funnel 
warm/moist air from the Gulf into the area, pivoting around an 
upper ridge centered to our southwest across the western 
Tennessee Valley. This continued moisture return has 
facilitated slightly more widespread river valley fog this 
morning, once again primarily south of the Ohio River where BL 
flow is weaker. A gradual expansion in coverage may continue to 
occur until dawn, with dense fog possible in the usual areas.

The aforementioned frontal boundary will begin to creep
southward today as a cold front, gradually crossing through the
CWA beginning tonight through midday on Friday. The front is
then progged to stall southwest of the area late Friday into 
Saturday, then quickly buckle back north as a warm front late 
Saturday and Saturday night, then once again become quasi- 
stationary just north or across the forecast area into early 
next week. This all translates into a generally active pattern 
across the CWA, with daily rain chances amid warm/humid 
conditions, into at least early next week. The primary concerns
with this pattern will continue to be the potential for 
localized flash flooding and isolated strong diurnal storms at
times. A more robust shortwave may eventually help clear the 
area out from showers/storms sometime mid to late next week.

Rain chances will be highly correlated to the position of the 
frontal boundary, and enhanced by diurnal heating or at times
weak crossing upper-level perturbations atop the aforementioned
ridge. Given the overall recent wet pattern we've been in over
the last week or two, and the return of a very moist (Gulf
influenced) airmass with progged PWATs pushing 1.7-2.1" at 
times (00Z ILN RAOB - 2.04"), the concern for flash flooding 
will return. The period of greatest concern in the near term is 
later today into tonight with the potential for heavy shower 
and thunderstorm activity via diurnal heating and a weak 
crossing upper wave. One hour FFG remains relatively low across 
most northern zones at less than 1.5", with just slightly 
higher values further south. CAMs however continue to depict 
significant spread in progged rainfall amounts, with confidence
in placement of any heavier rainfall corridors remaining 
relatively low. For example, 00Z HREF probabilities of 1.5"/hr 
in a 25-mile radius are generally less than 10%. While this 
doesn't rule out the potential for isolated instances of flash 
flooding today/tonight, it does result in confidence that is 
too low for a Flood Watch at this time. WPC has maintained a 
Marginal Risk for excessive rainfall across much of the area
today into tonight. A general reprieve is expected on Friday, 
with isolated to scattered shower/storm chances across the south
and mountains. A mainly dry day is expected on Saturday, with 
increasing shower/storm chances Saturday night through Sunday as
the front lifts back north across the area, with localized 
flash flooding once again being possible.

The other aspect of this pattern will be the potential for 
isolated strong diurnal thunderstorms at times, once again 
hinging on the position of the frontal boundary. The general 
setup will feature modest shear (15-25 kts / 0-6km) and modest 
buoyancy (750-1,500 Mixed-layer CAPE) amid rather saturated 
profiles. A few isolated strong storms remain possible this
afternoon/evening, main hazard being strong wind gusts via wet
downbursts. Additional strong diurnal storm potential could 
return Sunday or early next week given slightly more favorable 
progged kinematics, but will once again hinge on the front's 
position in relation to the CWA.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Oppressive heat and humidity will continue today across portions
of the area in advance of the aforementioned cold front across 
the northern Ohio Valley. Increased cloud cover and rain chances
this afternoon/evening will temper the overall coverage of 
oppressive conditions across the lowlands from that of 
yesterday, existing today more so across our central/southern 
zones, where highs will once again reach the upper 80s to low 
90s, while mid 80s are expected across the northern lowlands. 
Have once again lowered dew points from central guidance this 
afternoon/evening, generally expecting values in the low 70s. 
The combination of aforementioned temperatures and dew points 
will result in heat indices this afternoon and early evening 
reaching the mid 90s to 100 across the central/southern 
lowlands, with an SPS potentially being issued later to 
highlight this. Be sure to take frequent breaks if outside 
during peak heating hours today.
